analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using noncompete agreements to block workers from taking new jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in February 2023, then sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make noncompete agreements — contracts that stop workers from taking a similar job at a rival company or starting their own business after they leave — unenforceable and illegal for future agreements. It keeps narrow carve-outs: sellers of a business can still agree not to compete against the buyer, top executives can get a noncompete for up to one year as part of a sale if they receive severance pay, and partners leaving a partnership can be restricted. Employers would have to post workplace notices that noncompetes are banned, the Federal Trade Commission and Labor Department would both enforce the ban, and workers, state attorneys general, and courts would be able to sue violators. The bill would also void agreements that force workers into arbitration or give up class actions over noncompete violations, while leaving trade secret and nondisclosure protections untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly one in five American workers is covered by a noncompete agreement, according to economists cited in the bill's own findings. Those workers would gain the freedom to change jobs, negotiate higher pay, or start businesses in their own field without fear of being sued. Job seekers and rival employers would also gain access to a pool of experienced workers currently locked in place.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids future noncompete agreements for ordinary employees and contract workers, and the bill's findings cite economists estimating that 1 in 5 workers is currently covered by one [S3].

Enforcement would have teeth: the FTC could treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, the Labor Department could investigate and sue on workers' behalf, individual workers could sue for actual damages plus attorney's fees, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents [S2][S3].
Workers could not be forced into arbitration or blocked from class actions over noncompete violations, which matters because an individual worker suing an employer alone is often outmatched [S3].

Employers would keep the tools they have to protect genuinely sensitive business information — trade secrets, intellectual property, and nondisclosure agreements — so the ban targets the broad mobility restrictions, not legitimate confidentiality [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompetes to hold down wages and keep trained workers from moving to competitors would lose that leverage. Some businesses argue they need noncompetes to protect training investments; the bill's answer is that trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements cover that.

drawbacks.text: Employers who invest in training workers would lose a tool they say protects that investment; the bill's counterargument, spelled out in its own findings, is that narrower legal tools like trade secrets and NDAs already exist for legitimate interests [S3].

The bill allows noncompetes for top executives as part of business sales — a carve-out that critics of noncompetes say preserves the restriction where the executives negotiating deals can most afford to protect themselves, while rank-and-file workers get none [S3].

Splitting enforcement between the FTC and the Labor Department requires the two agencies to write shared standards within a year and the Labor Department to issue regulations within 18 months, a layering of agencies that could slow or muddle enforcement in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring job mobility and bargaining power to a fifth of the workforce — is broad and documented in the bill's own findings, which link noncompetes to lower wages and slower innovation. The real costs fall on employers who lose a cheap way to retain staff, and the executive carve-out is an honest reason to object. On balance the design is coherent: it bans the broad restriction while leaving targeted protections intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, bounced to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 1, 2023 by Rep. Scott Peters with Reps. Gallagher and Eshoo as original cosponsors, giving it sponsorship from both parties [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced; no action followed [S5].
On February 10, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where the action history ends [S5].
Cosponsorship stayed at three members and no vote ever occurred in either chamber through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements to keep workers from leaving kept a legal tool that suppresses wages and job mobility, because nothing changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that use noncompetes; workers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — one Democrat and two Republicans as original cosponsors — but with only three cosponsors total, neither party ever brought it to a vote, so no party breakdown of a vote exists.

industries.note: The bill strips employers of the ability to bind workers — whom economists cited in the bill say number 1 in 5 across sectors and income levels — with post-employment restrictions. Its loss is workers' gain: the agreements reduce wages and mobility. [S3]

industries.industry: Rival employers and competitors of covered firms
industries.note: Firms competing for talent would gain access to experienced workers currently locked in place, and could hire them without fear of litigation. This is the competition channel the bill is designed to open. [S3]

industries.industry: Buyers and sellers of businesses (including private equity and strategic acquirers)
industries.note: The bill preserves the traditional sale-of-business exception, so noncompetes stay available when a company is sold — the carve-out that makes the ban tolerable to dealmaking interests while ordinary workers get none. [S3]
